Bogle bursts forward on the right flank and fires a powerful, teasing cross towards the back post. Okafor makes the run, but Sadiki is there to make a terrific interception and clear the danger.

Sunderland take advantage of the windy conditions as Trafford flaps at Xhaka’s looped corner. The ball drops to Angulo, whose low, driven half-volley is blocked by a sea of Leeds bodies.

Le Fee tries to slide an intricate pass through to Tutierov, but it’s cut out by Bijol, who reads the situation well.

Bogle catches Reinildo above his hip with a high boot. The referee gives the Leeds man a yellow card. Sunderland want something more. That was certainly a risky tackle from Bogle, who now must be careful.

Let's go, Timur 👊 https://t.co/JVxgPM7zAC

Attacking changes are here for both sides. Brobbey’s Sunderland return lasts for over an hour and he’s replaced by Tutierov. Meanwhile, for the visitors, Wilson and Aaronson depart for Stach and Okafor.

Bogle carelessly catches Angulo with a late tackle, gifting Sunderland a great chance to swing the ball into the box. Le Fee whips it in, but its flicked on and goes out for a goal kick.

This game is now being played at a much quicker tempo, with Justin bending an effort towards the far top corner. However, it drifts wide. Both sides look far more confident now and not like they’re playing for a draw.

At the other end, the ball breaks to Angulo, who stings Trafford’s palms with a fierce curling strike that forces the Leeds goalkeeper into conceding a corner. Excitement in this second half is starting to ramp up.

Leeds come forward again as Bogle tries to slide a low cross into Tanaka, but Le Fee tracks back to prevent the visitors from getting a shot off.

Wilson whips in a deep corner. Muharemovic wins the header at the back stick, but can’t get threatening contact on it and slowly directs it into Roefs’ grasp.

If I’m being kind to the players out there, playing in a strong wind at the Stadium of Light is notoriously tricky.

If you are watching on television, you might have noticed in the first half the litter being blown around in circles on the pitch. That will give you an idea of the conditions. The wind tends to swirl around inside this stadium rather than blowing in one direction. If I were any good at physics I would be able to tell you why. But I’m not. So I can’t.

Still, this match is yet to strike an attacking rhythm. Leeds have dominated the ball since the break, with Mukiele’s injury and subsequent departure slightly unsettling the hosts. Aaronson acrobatically knocks the ball across the six-yard box, but it’s hooked clear by Sunderland.

Mukiele won’t return to the action and heads down the tunnel. Alderete is on to replace his fellow defender. That is a blow for Sunderland to lose Mukiele this early in the second half.

We're forced into a change 🔄 https://t.co/ZJB0NOnawt

Mukiele is sat up and is still receiving treatment after being caught by O’Nein on his Adam’s apple. He walks off the pitch and it’s unclear if he’s able to continue. For now, Sunderland are down to 10 men.

The medical staff are waved on to the pitch as O’Nein accidentally catches Mukiele in the face with his outstretched arm.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Only two shots on target in that first half, with Brobbey forcing a couple of saves from Trafford. Hopefully we’re treated to some more exciting football after the break.

In a game lacking creativity and chances, nothing separates Sunderland and Leeds at the break. The best chance of the first half fell to Brobbey, but Trafford did well to smother the one-on-one opportunity.

There will be just one minute of added time to end this first half.

Nearly a disaster at the back for Sunderland as O’Nein lets a ball run thinking Roefs will come out to clear. However, the goalkeeper stays put. With Calvert-Lewin closing in, O’Nein has to make a last-ditch sliding challenge to direct the ball back to Roefs to stop the striker in his tracks.

Reinildo is booked as Bogle turns him, with the Sunderland defender dragging the Leeds man to the florr. He protests his innocence, and in fairness to Reinildo, he has a ripped shirt. He must be freezing.

Hume draws huge applause from the home fans as he crunches into a challenge on Gudmundsson. The Sunderland fans loved that sliding tackle.

Leeds are still waiting to record a shot on target. They’ve been pretty safe and unadventurous in forward areas so far.

A lot of huff and puff, honest endeavour and robust challenges in this game so far, but the two moments of quality have come from Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford. His first save to deny Brian Brobbey was excellent. He perfectly judged the trajectory of an awkward bouncing ball at full stretch, but I think the second is even better.

Trafford was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international but the way he stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb. He may have saved with his feet, but he cramped Brobbey for room and timed his moment to dive at his feet perfectly. That was elite level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Ampadu picks up the game’s first yellow card for bumping into Angulo on the edge of his own box. Sunderland now have a free kick in a promising position. Unfortunately for the hosts, Le Fee smacks it straight into the wall.

Sunderland’s pressure nearly pays off as Xhaka forces Wilson into a mistake. Brobbey is then too strong for Bijol and shrugs the defender off the ball. From a tight angle, the striker has a one-on-one opportunity against Trafford, but the Leeds goalkeeper does well to block Brobbey’s side-footed effort.

Sunderland fans are urging their side to press at every opportunity, cheering each time an intervention is successful. Still, we wait for the first notable chance.

Mukiele is down after being caught in the face by Calvert-Lewin as they both challenged for a high ball. There was no malice in the striker’s attempt to win possession and play swiftly continues following some quick treatment for Mukiele.

Mukiele was gearing up for a long throw, but the Sunderland defender held onto the ball for too long, with referee Attwell sounding his whistle to give possession back to Leeds.

Ampadu’s long throw-in casuses some momentary chaos in Sunderland’s six-yard box. However, the linesman’s flag is raised and Leeds’ chance disappears.

It’s been a scrappy opening to this game. Mukiele tries a very ambitious effort from long range, but he drags the shot well wide and it harmlessly trickles out of play.

O’Nein defends unconvincingly as he battles with Calvert-Lewin and attempts to deal with a long ball. The centre back just about handles the situation and prevents the striker from carving out a one-on-one opportunity.

On his return to the Sunderland line-up, Brobbey tests Trafford in Sunderland’s first attack. The striker’s deflected effort bounces awkwardly in front of the goalkeeper, who parries the ball out for a corner. Leeds then defend the set-piece well and clear the danger.

That was a deceptively hard save for James Trafford to make to deny Brian Brobbey. Although the connection was not the cleanest, that almost made it harder as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the England international meant he had to watch it all the way and keep a strong hand at full stretch. Excellent work from the summer signing from Manchester City.

Leeds are dominating the ball in these early exchanges. Sunderland look slightly unsettled so far. Bogle is pushing particularly far forward for the visitors.

Wilson starts for Leeds. The Welshman was pivotal for Fulham last season. His Leeds career is yet to meaningfully get going, but he has a great chance to impress today.

Leeds get us under way here. How will come out on top in these feisty northern weather conditions?

My favourite part of every Sunderland game is the singing of Elvis Presley’ Can’t Help Falling in Love before kick off. Not sure the “The King” had a football club on Wearside in mind when he wrote it but it just works as a pre-match anthem. I also grew up in a house where there was a lot of Elivs playing when I was a small child. Anyway, on to the football.

The Stadium of Light is in fantastic spirits as per usual, despite Sunderland floundering in 20th position. Can the home side record a much-needed win to ignite their domestic season?

Starting good in the season, we are really keen to follow our goals for our system where we train every week and we follow how our team should play.

And, how the XI plus the subs should play together, fight for each other, and we have to keep on going like this. We know how good Sunderland are.

The team is good. Obviously, every team has a different start in the season but still we know what this team can do. Last year they achieved Europe so it is a really big thing.

We know the players and, yeah, we know how hard these games can be but we are here to try to win and to take all the points.

It is going to be a tough one. Also, the weather, I think. The wind is unbelievable but we are ready. We are here and ready to fight.

We go into every game confident and ready to fight for the three points. We are here to win. We are going for every game [because] we want to win so we will try our best and fight.

Right now, I think his intensity against the ball, his workload against the ball, is on a way better level in comparison to how it was when he arrived and as soon as he adapts, I’m pretty sure his quality will shine through sooner rather than later.

Leeds are always a good side, it was in the Championship and now in the Premier League.

They are doing really well, they are consistent as well. They built momentum early in the season, which is always good, so they are in a different position but anything is possible in football. We think that it is going to be a new opportunity to get better.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Sunderland: Roefs, Hume, Mukiele, O’Nien, Reinildo, Xhaka, Sadiki, Le Fée, Rigg, Angulo, BrobbeySubs: Ellborg, Methalie, Alderete, Diarra, Ahoka, Talbi, Fofana, Angulo, Tuterov

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1221. Man Utd Fans Slam ‘Embarrassing’ Player After 2-2 Sporting CP Draw

In their second game since Mauricio Pochettino took over from Michael Carrick, Manchester United took on Sporting CP. The Red Devils had to settle for a point in a 2-2 draw.

Having been thumped 4-0 by Liverpool in his first match in charge, the Argentine would have been desperate for a fast start in the Champions League. The first half, however, did not go to plan as the Red Devils conceded two penalties.

After Lisandro Martinez gave away the first, Senne Lammens made a save from 12 yards but then conceded another penalty only minutes later. This time, Sporting star Luis Suarez made no mistake, as he scored the second of his two spot kicks.

After the break, Martinez won the third penalty of the game, this time for the Red Devils when he was tripped in the box. Bruno Fernandes tucked home the first goal of the Pochettino era and then gave Man Utd a lead just two minutes later. His tame shot from the edge of the box took a strange deflection off a divot in the ground, and somehow found the back of the net.

United looked in control, but with 10 minutes to go, Lammens made a complete mess of claiming a cross, fumbling the ball. Suarez reacted brilliantly to acrobatically make it 2-2. Pochettino's men thought they'd taken a lead shortly after, but VAR intervened to rule out a goal after Kaique Pereira was deemed to have been fouled when trying to claim a corner.

There was then time for Youri Tielemans to get himself sent off late on for a second bookable offence, as the game ended 2-2. Man Utd fans will have to wait a little longer before seeing their first win under Pochettino.

While there was plenty of anger aimed at Lammens after the goalkeeper's errors, another player has also been blamed for the disappointing draw.

Despite Lammens having a horror display, giving away a penalty and then being at fault for the second goal as well, many Man Utd fans online instead turned their fury on Noussair Mazraoui. Starting ahead of the much-maligned Diogo Dalot, the Moroccan didn't fare any better.

Mazraoui lasted just 64 minutes before being replaced by the Portugal international. Unimpressed with his efforts, supporters on social media tore into the right-back, with one remarking:

"If Mazraoui starts next season with us, then I'll have no choice but to consider the Manchester United board shameless. Man has been dropping stinkers in almost every game."

Another added: "Dalot is worse than Mazraoui but Mazraoui is also worse than Dalot." While a third wrote: "Dalot in 5 mins has shown why he is far better than Mazraoui."

Someone added: "Mazraoui is trash guys we gave to accept it." Another summed up the mood, writing: "Mazraoui was not good enough for Bayern, what made the board think he’d be good enough for United?"

One more added: "Just keeps getting worse every week, Martinez & Mazraoui are embarrassing."

#1220. Guardiola explains to Romario why he should be patient with Ancelotti

Pep Guardiola defended Carlo Ancelotti during an interview with Brazil legend Romario, explaining to his former Barcelona teammate why he should be patient with the Italian tactician: ‘How many World Cups has Brazil played?’

Romario has been one of Ancelotti’s harshest critics, especially after the Seleçao’s elimination from the 2026 World Cup Round of 16.

Guardiola has faced Ancelotti’s teams many times and clearly doesn’t share his former Barcelona teammate’s view.

“How many World Cups has Brazil played? Million! You’ve lost more than you’ve won,” Guardiola said.

Romario argued that he’s not annoyed that Brazil don’t win, but by the way they play.

“I’ve coached Brazilian players, and everyone says the pressure here is greater than anywhere else. It’s very hard,” Guardiola replied.

“I know Carlo a bit. I’ve played against him many times; he’s beaten me a million times. He’s an extraordinary person, and I have no doubt about his ability. He’s come to a new country, to a new culture, and sometimes you need a bit more time. You know there isn’t enough time to train a national team. We’ll see what happens.

“[It happens to] most of the coaches who go from a club to a national team for the first time. I believe that, in the end, football is football; you have less time and have to adapt, but I’m sorry, Mario, I couldn’t doubt Carlo’s ability; it’s impossible, impossible. I know him. People say, ‘He’s good at managing the group’; everyone says he’s the best. I faced him, and he’s very smart. He makes tactical decisions. He knows, as I do, that if you don’t win, you won’t last. Why did I stay at Manchester City for so many years? Because we won a lot. If not, you go home.”

Romario and Guardiola also spoke about their defeat in the 1994 Champions League Final against Fabio Capello’s Milan.

Romario asked Pep whether that Milan side were technically stronger than their Barcelona, but Pep seemed unsure.

“They were very strong, very, very strong. We were too, but they were really strong,” he said.

“It’s very hard with Italian football. Capello had his way of playing, different from Johan’s [Cruijff], but they were a top side.”

In the same interview, Guardiola spoke for the first time about rejecting an offer to coach Italy’s national team last summer, saying he needed to rest and admitting he could have accepted the proposal if it had come at a different time in his life.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1219. Arsenal Thought They Signed a 'Phenom' in Miyaichi, but things went wrong

Back in 2011, Arsenal had built up a reputation for identifying some of the most talented players, whether it was Nicolas Anelka, Aaron Ramsey or Theo Walcott. The Gunners did some wise business, and they thought they had done the same with Ryo Miyaichi when they plucked from obscurity in 2011, offering him a trial.

Arséne Wenger was impressed by Miyachi when he had a trial with the club, and he offered the Japanese youngster a professional contract at the end of January of 2011.

The Frenchman said at the time: "We’re delighted that Ryō Miyaichi has joined us. He trialed with us in the summer and has raw ability which has attracted many clubs around the world". Some believed at the time that he could be the 'next Lionel Messi'.

"Ryo has natural technical ability. He has good balance and phenomenal pace, and his passing and crossing is consistently of a high quality. He is a very exciting player." - Wenger on Miyaichi in 2011

Miyaichi was an ultra-skillful player who quickly impressed in the youth ranks, both for club and country, and he was on course to become a star. In fact, during his first senior spell in professional football, on loan at Feyenoord, he was nicknamed 'Ryodinho' by the Dutch media, which only sparked excitement among Arsenal fans.

"I like his pace, his mobility and his movement off the ball. I like players who can move when others have the ball. There is also his attitude, commitment and desire. That is why I decided to keep him." - Wenger on Miyaichi in 2011

He went on to spend time at Bolton Wanderers and then Wigan Athletic, where he suffered a long-term ankle injury that saw him miss their successful FA Cup campaign.

By this point, Miyaichi had managed just one senior league appearance for Arsenal, and after a loan spell with Twente back in the Netherlands, he was released by the Gunners. Miyaichi later reflected: "Back then, I didn't really think of myself as young. There were so many world-class players around my age, and I was always feeling pressed."

The Japan international found a new permanent home at St Pauli, but his debut was significantly delayed by an ACL rupture, and after returning to action, he ruptured the ACL in his other leg in a horrible run of luck.

Remarkably, the German side still renewed the winger's contract. Sporting chief Andreas Rettig explained: “Ryo has unbelievable bad luck, and we do not want to leave him alone. [We want to] show that we are behind him. We hope that this decision will help Ryo to return to his old level of performance.”

Reflecting on his career at a later date, Miyaichi went on to say: "At one point, I seriously thought about quitting soccer.

"I have been away from the team for long periods and have caused trouble time and again. I have also disappointed many people. That is why I thought about quitting."

He went on to enjoy a couple of seasons of full fitness before being released in 2021 after racking up 77 league appearances. It was at that stage that he returned to Japan, joining Yokohoma F. Marinos, where he has been since, racking up 104 league appearances and scoring eight times. Back in 2022, he actually added three more Japan caps to his name, which must have been nice for him after all the injury troubles that followed his first two caps in 2012.

At 33 years of age, Miyaichi is still playing with Yokohoma F. Marinos, and he won the JLeague with them back in 2022, adding to the two FA Cups he technically won between Wigan in 2013 and Arsenal in 2014.

Speaking back in June on why he wants to keep playing, Miyaichi said: "I think having fun is the most important thing. It's what fuels your growth. I still have the desire to keep improving and still feel the same way I always did. Showing people something that makes them think is cool on the pitch is what I'm there for."

Miyaichi's never-ending battles with injury must have made for a tough time, but fueled by his love for the game, he never gave up, and perseverance has allowed him to keep playing at the age of 33. Things could have gone a very different way for the winger, even if his biggest hopes were not fulfilled.

Tzolis' 64% pass rate and 16 turnovers underlined a stale forward line, forcing Arteta into a risky selection call.

#1218. US Police Share Statement as English Footballer Shot and Killed in Mississippi

Tragic reports have emerged from the United States, confirming that a young English footballer was shot and killed in Mississippi. The local police have now shared a statement after making an arrest.

Krissh Mahatma was born in London but had moved to the US to pursue his dream of making it as a footballer. The 18-year-old striker was in his freshman year at Copiah-Lincoln Community College in Wesson, around 45 miles south of Jackson, Mississippi, where the incident took place.

Before moving to the US, he had played for Watford 'A' in the post-16 Community and Education Football Alliance league. Co-Lin announced his signing in February.

As reported by the Daily Mail, Mahatma was fatally struck by a bullet after a gun was fired outside the Green Ghost Tacos restaurant in Jackson at around 3:39 a.m. on Sunday morning.

The English footballer was with his Co-Lin Wolves teammates when they reportedly came across a drunk man outside the restaurant. After a fight broke out, a man pulled out a gun and fired into the group, hitting Mahatma.

The 18-year-old was taken to a nearby hospital via a private vehicle. According to Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard, this was where he died.

Capitol Police have since arrested and charged Danny Luna, 22, with murder. The Mississippi Department of Public Safety did not elaborate on what caused the deadly confrontation. However, in a brief statement, Police Chief Mark Miller sent 'thoughts and prayers' to Mahatma's 'family and loved ones,' adding:

"While this arrest is an important step toward justice, we recognise that nothing can ease the pain of losing a loved one."

Is the Premier League really the best in the world?

Mahatma had made 14 appearances in his first three months with the Co-Lin Wolves, scoring one goal in September in a 3-2 win over National Park College. Co-Lin president Dewayne Middleton issued his own statement on behalf of the college:

"Copiah-Lincoln Community College is mourning the loss of freshman soccer player Krissh Mahatma. Krissh will be deeply missed by his teammates and the entire Co-Lin family."

A fundraiser has been set up to support Mahatma's family and has already raised $31,851 (£24,275). It explained how the young striker was "just beginning a new chapter of life far away from home," before adding: "His sudden passing has left his family, friends, teammates, coaches, and the entire Co-Lin soccer community heartbroken.

"Behind this tragedy is a family grieving the loss of their son and loved ones trying to make sense of a loss that feels impossible to put into words."

The owner of the Green Ghost Tacos eatery, nearby where the shooting took place, said: "On behalf of the entire Green Ghost family, I extend my deepest and most heartfelt condolences to the family, friends, loved ones, and university community mourning the tragic loss of a young student. Our hearts are heavy, and our thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected by this devastating incident.

"While this tragedy occurred near our establishment, we would like to clarify that Green Ghost was closed and was not conducting business at the time of the shooting. The safety and well-being of our patrons, employees, and surrounding community remain a top priority. We are committed to cooperating fully with law enforcement as they investigate the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident.

"Out of respect for the grieving family and the investigation, we will refrain from speculating or commenting further on the details at this time. Above all, we recognise that a family has suffered an unimaginable loss. We ask that the community join us in extending compassion, prayers, and support to those affected during this incredibly difficult time."

#1217. Neto: ‘Excited’ to play for Juventus again after almost ten years

Brazilian goalkeeper Neto will start for Juventus in a Europa League game against Omonia FC tomorrow: ‘I’m really excited to be back on the pitch.’

The experienced goalkeeper returned to Turin on a free transfer in September, replacing the injured Kamil Grabara.

The Poland international suffered a season-ending knee injury, urging Juventus to sign a replacement.

Neto has not played a competitive match since May 30 with Botafogo, and last played for Juventus nearly ten years ago, in May 2017, helping them beat Lazio 2-0 in a Coppa Italia Final.

“It’s hugely satisfying. I’m really excited to be back on the pitch, and proud to be part of this team,” Neto said at a press conference today, as quoted by Ilbianconero.com.

“Football and life go through different cycles, and there are different people involved. I see a very healthy environment for achieving our goals, and that’s what we need to maintain: the belief that we’re on the right track.

“I was at a point where I was looking for certain things, and whatever I did in the next stage of my life had to make sense,” he added when asked about his return to Juventus.

“I was looking for something that would inspire me. When this opportunity came along, I felt that. It had a different meaning. Deep down, I felt my chapter with Juve was still open.

“I’m very happy and satisfied. I enjoy my work, and whatever comes in the future is in God’s hands. I’m here to help, and whatever happens will happen.

“We’re in a place where, wherever you look, you see so many trophies. Whether we talk about it or not, there’s no need to spell it out: we know where we are and what we represent. I’m here to try to achieve great results, and I sense the same ambition around me. Hopefully we can get there. Just like the other teams, we want to win. That’s what we’re fighting for.”

Juventus sit fifth in the Europa League standings with ten points in four matches, but have had very different results in Serie A, where they have already lost three games from 12 and sit 6th in the table, six points behind Milan in four.

Neto, however, has plenty of confidence in his teammates.

“Seeing and feeling the desire these lads have, with so many young players willing to contribute, is truly infectious. From my perspective, that’s a positive thing,” the 37-year-old said.

“There are important players here. We’re talking about Juve. We have the team, the desire and the determination, and hopefully we can get there.

“Every competition is difficult these days. We are Juventus, and whenever Juventus play, we have a responsibility to compete to win. That’s our goal. I haven’t looked at what lies ahead, because at this club you have to fight to win. That’s how it is for me, and I imagine it’s the same for everyone.

“This is a developing team with lots of young players who may be playing in this league for the first time and are still finding their feet. There can be ups and downs. The season is so long that we can’t focus solely on this moment, because in a month we might be talking about something else. My focus is always on giving 100% in training. We need to find balance and consistency.”

Omonia FC have grabbed two wins and two defeats in four Europa League games so far and sit 18th in the table.

“It will be a difficult match. They’re a very strong team,” insisted Neto.

“We’ve watched them, and they counterattack with real quality. I know Fabiano from our time in Brazil. Every game in Europe is difficult, and we know the challenges involved.”

Juventus’ first-choice goalkeeper Vicario will rest tomorrow. He’s on loan from Tottenham, but does he deserve to remain at Juventus long-term?

“I don’t know how much my opinion matters, but he’s a top-level goalkeeper,” Neto concluded.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1216. Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Vertebrate trunk development is orchestrated by endogenous signalling centres that generate gradients of signals such as WNT and BMP to pattern cell fates and drive morphogenesis1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Whether these cues alone can reconstitute human trunk-like morphogenesis in vitro remains unknown. Here we present a synthetic embryology platform for high-throughput, spatiotemporal delivery of morphogen signals to epithelial cysts derived from human pluripotent stem cells. Transient WNT and BMP gradients are sufficient to drive the generation of axially elongating trunk-like structures that contain a central neural tube flanked by axial, paraxial, intermediate and lateral mesoderm. The geometry of the transient BMP signal exerts lasting control over mediolateral patterning and bilateral symmetry. Patterning and morphogenesis are sustained by neuromesodermal and lateral plate mesoderm progenitors induced by the initial cues, which act as endogenous signalling centres. Together, these findings define a minimal spatial code sufficient to reconstitute trunk-like morphogenesis in a human stem-cell-based model and establish a scalable platform for studying early human development and congenital disorders.

The scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data generated for this study are available from the GEO under accessions GSE306808 and GSE347564, respectively. Sequencing reads were aligned to the GRCh38 human reference genome (10x Genomics GRCh38-2020 for scRNA-seq; Ensembl GRCh38, assembly accession GCA_000001405.29, for bulk RNA-seq). Previously published29 human embryo scRNA-seq data are available from the GEO under accession GSE155121. Other reanalysed datasets are available from the following repositories: mouse gastrulation, ArrayExpress (E-MTAB-6967)55; cynomolgus macaque embryo, GEO (GSE193007)56; RA-gastruloid, GEO (GSE208369)57; axial organoid, GEO (GSE220563)17; axioloid, GEO (GSE199576)18; and segmentoid, GEO (GSE195467)19. GEO series are accessible at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ and ArrayExpress experiments at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/arrayexpress. The confocal and time-lapse datasets are large multichannel image series that are impractical to deposit in full; the measurement tables from which the quantitative imaging panels are plotted are provided in the code repository (Code availability). Raw imaging data, and any additional information required to reanalyse the data reported in this study, are available from the lead contact, S.R., on request; requests will be answered within 1 month and data shared by secure electronic file transfer without restriction. Source data are provided with this paper.

Custom code for image analysis and for bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq analysis—including SMD feature selection, clustering and annotation, and the trunk morph–embryo correspondence analyses—is available under the MIT License at GitHub (https://github.com/stevenzwick/zwick-2026-trunk-morphogenesis) and archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22756590)58. Random seeds and exact parameters (intensity thresholds and gates, background offsets, local-threshold window sizes, Gaussian σ, histogram edges, clustering resolutions and curated gene lists) are provided in the repository.

a, A detailed schematic of the workflow is shown: (i) Matrigel is microcontact printed onto the two-layered PDMS stamp (PDMS-ii) using a flat PDMS stamp (PDMS-i). (ii) A thin PDMS microwell array is peeled from the silicon master and overlaid on a glass coverslip. Taller PDMS sidewalls are plasma-bonded along two edges. (iii) Capillary water flow through the microchannels drives localized Matrigel transfer from stamp PDMS-ii onto the PDMS microwell layer at the contact interface. (iv) Cells are seeded onto the transferred Matrigel pattern, overlaid with a silanized coverslip atop the sidewalls, and cultured further with media and microwell-trapped beads. b, Photographs of the experimental setup corresponding to steps a(i–iii): coating the flat stamp (grey border, fourth column, top); PDMS-ii stamps with different patterns (blue border, first column); PDMS microwell layer with wells at different positions (red border, second column); aligned PDMS-ii stamp and PDMS microwell layer in contact (green border, third column); and the application of weight and water flow for transfer (green border, fourth column, bottom). MG, Matrigel; RT, room temperature.

a–d, Design of two-layer PDMS stamp and microwell substrate: a, upper-layer pattern used to print Matrigel features; b, lower-layer embedded microchannels (white denotes channel features); c, assembled two-layer PDMS stamp with a three-dimensional illustration of the assembled stamp below; d, alignment of stamp features and microwell layer, with 120 µm diameter microwells positioned at defined distances from pattern edges. Scale bars, 1 mm. e, Whole-chip images show humidified microcontact printing (HµCP) of Matrigel mixed with fluorescently conjugated BSA (cyan) onto PDMS microwell chip (brightfield, grey), using a four-square stamp pattern. Air bubbles beneath PDMS microwell layer and above glass coverslip are visible in brightfield images. Images are representative of 6 independent experiments (12 chips) with similar results. Scale bars, 1 mm. f, Whole-chip image shows standard microcontact printing (µCP) of fluorescent BSA onto glass to validate stamp pattern from a. Image is representative of 2 independent experiments (5 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. g, Image shows pluripotent epithelial cysts formed 3 days after seeding on a PDMS microwell chip, using stamp pattern from a. A diversity of cyst arrangements, rather than the optimized hexagonal pattern with a central cyst as in Fig. 1, are used to show the flexibility of the approach. Image is representative of 79 independent experiments (145 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. h, Whole-chip epifluorescence image shows pluripotent cysts (DAPI, grey), well-trapped BMP4-coated beads (pseudocoloured red), and pSMAD1/5/9 immunofluorescence (pSMAD, green) 6 h after bead deposition. Image is representative of 6 independent experiments (13 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. i, Representative higher magnification images of cyst arrays with adjacent BMP beads and pSMAD1/5/9 immunofluorescence 6 h after bead deposition, from three independent experiments. (Top row) Five-cyst arrays with one or two beads, from chip in h. (Bottom left) Seven-cyst array with two beads, from an independent experiment. (Bottom right) Five-cyst array with three beads, from an independent experiment. Scale bars, 100 µm. j, (Left) Plot shows normalized pSMAD1/5/9 intensity (pSMAD/DAPI) versus distance from BMP bead, d, for all cysts from chip in h except cysts at centre of arrays (n = 201 cysts; light grey lines, individual cyst profiles; solid lines, mean; shaded areas, ±1 s.d.). (Right) pSMAD1/5/9 intensity in the bead-proximal epithelium of each cyst is plotted against the distance to the nearest bead, dmin, showing a negative correlation (red line, R2 = 0.624; n = 156 cysts) up to a distance of 635 µm, beyond which the intensity is low and uncorrelated (R2 = 0.061; n = 45 cysts). k, (Left) Normalized pSMAD1/5/9 is plotted against angle relative to bead direction (θ - θb) for cysts within responsive regime (d < 635 µm; n = 156 cysts). (Right) The direction of the pSMAD1/5/9 distribution, quantified by its first moment, is plotted as a function of the angle towards the nearest bead, θb (R2 = 0.17, n = 156 cysts). The correlation between pSMAD1/5/9 direction and bead angle is weaker than in Fig. 1f due to the overlapping influence of multiple BMP beads positioned near most cyst arrays in h.

a, (top) Live YFP and merged Brightfield (BF)–YFP images show hexagonally arranged cysts derived from the BMP4-T2A-Achilles reporter hPSC line 6 h after exposure to BMP4-coated beads (pseudocoloured red), with no detectable YFP signal. Images are from one experiment (36 cyst arrays). (bottom) Live images of the cysts from (top) 24 h after bead exposure show the presence of YFP (arrowhead) in some cells adjacent to beads. Images are from one experiment (2 cyst arrays). b, Plot of BMP4 read counts per million (CPM) from bulk RNA sequencing of pluripotent cysts at 0 h, 7 h, and 24 h after BMP bead exposure (n = 3 biologically independent samples per timepoint). Dots, individual samples; bars, mean; error bars, ±1 s.d. BMP5 expression was not detected in any of the samples. c, (left) Brightfield, DAPI (grey) and definitive endoderm marker SOX17 immunofluorescence (cyan) images show spatially arranged cysts after a 2-day exposure to the main experimental conditions, including BMP bead exposure, WNT-driven symmetry breaking, and Activin/Nodal signalling inhibitor A83-01 (above), or without A83-01 (below). Images are from one experiment per condition (with A83-01: 1 chip, 21 cyst arrays; without A83-01: 2 chips, 47 cyst arrays). (right) Bulk RNA-seq analysis of key endodermal genes in cysts under the same two conditions, with (green, n = 3 biologically independent samples) or without A83-01 (purple, n = 2 biologically independent samples). Dots, individual samples; bars, mean; error bars, ±1 s.d. A83-01 prevents endoderm differentiation in all protocols here (Extended Data Fig. 5b, Fig. 4, Supplementary Data 5). d, (left) Plot of DAPI-normalized SOX2 and TBXT intensity versus distance from central cyst of array (“anterior”). TBXT varies more with distance from anterior than distance from bead (Fig. 2c) due to A–P symmetry breaking from geometric cyst arrangement16,17 (Fig. 1b). Black arrow indicates the regime where both TBXT and SOX2 are high, corresponding to NMP differentiation (n = 210 biologically independent cysts; thin lines, individual cyst profiles; thick line, mean; shaded area, 95% confidence interval). (right) Pixel density plot of normalized SOX2 versus TBXT; percentages, fractions of pixels above and below the cutoffs. 28% of pixels are SOX2+ TBXT+, indicative of NMP-like expression. e, Brightfield, DAPI (grey), and TBXT immunofluorescence (cyan) images of three hexagonal cyst arrays without (left) or with a central cyst (right) on the same chip. In the absence of the central cyst, hexagonal cysts are prone to express TBXT on both their inward- and outward-facing poles (white arrowheads), indicating a lack of clear A-P polarity. With the central cyst present, TBXT expression is restricted to the outward-facing pole. Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (12 cyst arrays) with similar results. f, Brightfield and immunofluorescence images of cysts after 2 days of differentiation show FOXF1+ nascent lateral plate mesoderm (LPM, red) proximal to BMP4-coated beads (pseudocoloured red; red arrows top left, white arrows elsewhere), whereas FOXA2+ anterior mesoderm (magenta) and SOX2+ neural progenitors (yellow) are distant from beads. Cysts are from another chip of the same design (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Images are representative of 3 independent experiments with similar results. g, Pixel-density plots of FOXA2 versus FOXF1 (top) and SOX2 versus FOXF1 (bottom) immunofluorescence in day 2 cysts, indicating mutual exclusivity. Colour, log-scaled pixel density normalized to the 99th percentile of bin density; contours, equally spaced iso-density lines; dashed lines, positivity thresholds; percentages, fraction of pixels in each quadrant. n = 7 biologically independent cysts from 3 independent experiments. h, Images of cysts after 2 days of differentiation show FOXF1+ nascent LPM located proximally to BMP beads, FOXA2+ anterior mesoderm distant from beads, and TBXT+ mesoderm at posterior end of cysts. Images are representative of 5 independent experiments with similar results. i, Per-chip fraction of cysts containing FOXF1:Achilles+ cells, plotted as in Fig. 2e, for each condition: adjacent to a BMP bead (“Bead”), no bead (“No Bead”) and adjacent to a bead following BMPR1A knockdown (“KD”). Dots, one chip from each of four independent experiments; bars, mean; error bars, ±1 s.d. across experiments. n = 182 (“Bead”), 1,010 (“No Bead”) and 189 (“KD”) cysts scored in total (see Methods, “Fraction of FOXF1+ cysts”). j, BMPR1A CPM from bulk RNA-seq of cells following BMPR1A knockdown compared with a scrambled control (n = 3 biologically independent samples per condition). Dots, individual samples; bars, mean; error bars, ±1 s.d. Two-sided Welch’s t-test: t = −7.00, d.f. = 2.5, P = 0.010, mean difference −28.1 CPM (95% CI, −42.3 to −13.9). *P < 0.05. k, Quantification of pSMAD1/5/9 in cells at the edge following 30 min treatment with 10 ng ml−1 BMP4. BMPR1A knockdown cells show reduced pSMAD1/5/9 compared with SCRAMBLE control cells (n = 3 biologically independent samples per condition). Additional quantification at different time points and cell locations is provided in Supplementary Data 4. Dots, per-well medians; centre line, median; boxes, interquartile range; whiskers, extreme values within 1.5× interquartile range. l, Representative immunostaining images for the analysis in k: BMPR1A knockdown (top row) and SCRAMBLE (bottom row); knockdown cells (CFP, yellow, left), DAPI (middle), and pSMAD1/5/9 (cyan, right). Images are from one experiment (3 wells each). m, Images show two additional replicates of day 2 morphs as in Fig. 2f, showing the co-expression of BMP4:Achilles (green) and FOXF1:mScarlet3 (red). Images are representative of 3 independent experiments (13 chips) with similar results. n, Fluorescent RNA in situ hybridization images for BMP4 (green) and FOXF1 (red) transcripts show co-localization in a bead-adjacent cyst after 2 days of differentiation. Representative image from n = 6 biologically independent bead-adjacent cysts. o, Pixel-density plot of FOXF1 versus BMP4 in situ signal in the day 2 cyst shown in n. Colour, log-scaled pixel density normalized to its maximum; contours, equally spaced iso-density lines. The two signals are positively correlated (R2 = 0.646). Scale bars, 100 µm.

a, A schematic of trunk morph differentiation protocol is shown. hPSCs were seeded onto micropatterned PDMS microwell substrate on Day −3 in mTeSR Plus with 10 µM Y-27632. The next day, Y-27632 was removed from media conditions and Matrigel added to induce the formation of single lumen epithelial cysts. On Day 0, BMP4-coated beads were injected into microwells, and cyst differentiation was initiated in N2B27 with 8–10 µM CHIR99021, 0.1–0.15 µM A83-01, and 50 ng ml−1 NOGGIN. After 48 h, cysts were transferred to individual wells in N2B27 with Matrigel and cultured for 3–4 days before analysis. b, Box-and-whisker plots show length of trunk morphs at 0, 48, and 120 h of differentiation. The same n = 93 biologically independent trunk morph samples were tracked across all three time points. #1215. 'You can't escape from it': Rasmus Hojlund opens up on the suffocating pressure of playing for Man United - and reveals Bruno Fernandes and Diogo Dalot are 'looking forward to change' under Mauricio Pochettino

Published: 05:31 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 06:12 EST, 25 November 2026

Rasmus Hojlund has laid bare the suffocating pressure of playing for Manchester United and given his insight into what Mauricio Pochettino’s squad will be suffering while marooned in the Premier League relegation zone.

The Dane was back in town this week after spending two seasons at United, mocking Manchester City fans when scoring the opener of Napoli’s 2-2 draw at the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday night.

Hojlund secured a £38million permanent move away from Old Trafford in the summer but remains in touch with plenty of old team-mates and believes the lack of equilibrium at the club has contributed to a steady decline.

‘There are so many people following the club around the world and you can’t really escape from it,’ Hojlund said.

‘It is almost too high when it is good and almost too low when it is bad. It is all about trying to be in that middle. I had both the highs and the lows there.

‘The pressure is part of the club, it comes with playing for United. There has been a lot of change but hopefully they will get it right with Mauricio.’

Rasmus Hojlund mocked Man City fans after scoring for Napoli at the Etihad on Tuesday night

A United supporter, Hojlund laughed off the idea that the club is in a relegation scrap despite their worst start to a season since 1972. And the 23-year-old revealed that the players were ready for ‘change’ following the sacking of Michael Carrick.

‘I spoke with Bruno [Fernandes] and Diogo [Dalot] during the international break and they were all obviously devastated that Michael was going but also looking forward to some change,’ Hojlund added.

‘I am still speaking with Patrick [Dorgu] and I just wish the guys all the best. I am sure they will turn it around this season. They have got a lot of quality. They have got a great squad, good leaders, good professionals.

‘It is a temporary picture, I think they will get back to the top. The Premier League is like this. I read the other day that Bournemouth was in the relegation zone after a couple of games, now they have won the last five games and are in the top half of the table.’

#1214. 25 Best Midfielders in the World Ranked (2026)

It's often said that whichever football team wins the battle of the midfield tends to win the game. Whether it's a holding midfielder who can shut down the opposition attack, an attacking one who can chip in with goals and assists, or a box-to-box player who can do both sides well effectively, they are usually the key to how a match pans out.

With that in mind, below are the 25 best midfielders in the world right now, ranked in order – and the level of talent is off the scale. The following factors have been taken into consideration when forming these rankings, with players such as Jude Bellingham and Bruno Fernandes featuring.

Arsenal, summer on summer, were looking for the final piece of the puzzle. Martin Zubimendi, signed from Real Sociedad in 2025, proved to be just that, with his willingness to screen the back four, allowing those ahead of him to be free in their attacking endeavours. Not only that, but his line-breaking passes are a sight to behold, and his defensively sound nature makes him the perfect midfielder beside Declan Rice.

Still just 27 years of age, the Spaniard has plenty of years left in the tank and was vital in the middle of the park for the Gunners as he helped the club end their Premier League title drought. He faded a little towards the end of his debut season, and has found his game time dwindle of late, but that doesn't take away from his class when at his best.

Still only 19 years old, Moroccan international Ayoubb Bouaddi has found himself thrusted into Manchester City's starting lineup alongside fellow new signing Elliot Anderson in recent weeks.

A composed, ball-carrying defensive midfielder who excels at receiving under pressure, dictating tempo, and breaking lines through dribbling rather than high-volume progressive passing - he's the kind of metronome that is rare in today's game. Even while the Cityzens have struggled for form as of late, the teenager has risen above the challenges thrown his way.

Ryan Gravenberch was one of Liverpool's best players under Arne Slot. The Dutchman was one of Jurgen Klopp's last signings but really flourished under his compatriot, who has now departed Anfield.

The confidence and calmness of his displays in the engine room, complemented by his running power that is very reminiscent of a certain Yaya Toure and neat spins reflective of old Anfield favourite Thiago Alcantara, have been a breath of fresh air for supporter. Even if Liverpool's form dropped off in 2025/26, he is easily among the finest midfielders in the world, though his defensive contributions have dried up in favour of adventure to bring about a side to his game that can be, at times, a little eccentric.

Scott McTominay enjoyed his career-best season in Italy under Antonio Conte just two seasons back, scoring 13 goals and providing six assists in 36 appearances across all competitions. He was instrumental in helping Napoli to their second Scudetto in three years, claiming the Serie A's Most Valuable Player award in the process.

The Scotland international could have only dreamt of times like these when he was operating as one-half of the infamous 'McFred' partnership during some of Manchester United's darkest hours in recent memory. But a disastrous World Cup campaign with the Tartan Army suggested that maybe Italy is just a safe haven for him, hence he's dropped down a few levels in this ranking since the last update.

One of the finest talents in the world, Bayern Munich's Jamal Musiala is only going to get better in the years to come. The Germany international looks set to be the heartbeat of his side at both club and international level, but is already producing the kind of end product that many players in their prime would be proud of. Not only is he used to getting on the scoresheet, but his dribbling ability is nothing short of otherworldly.

He is undeniably one of the brightest young players in world football, but Jamal Musiala chose to represent Germany over England - here's why.

If he continues at the pace he is currently going, then you would fancy him entering the Ballon d'Or conversation sooner rather than later. Musiala has done an admirable job from the left flank at times, but it's painfully obvious that his future lies in an attacking midfield role, and there's little doubt he will be one of the best in the world for the foreseeable future. He could be higher on this list if a recent injury hadn't hampered his progress, which lent itself to a poor World Cup cameo and a worrying start to the 2026/27 season, which has seen him fall out of favour in Bavaria.

Fabian Ruiz might not be as eye-catching as some of his Paris Saint-Germain teammates, hence his 24th-place finish in the 2025 Ballon d'Or race, but the role that the Spaniard plays in his side cannot be understated. The 30-year-old has been a consistent presence in Luis Enrique's team, providing balance to midfield and playing a crucial part in their domestic treble and Champions League success in 2024/25.

Ruiz played a key role as Spain won the 2026 World Cup, with head coach Luis de la Fuente often preferring the PSG star in midfield over Pedri. He's also won the Euros with La Roja, and the Nations League, and it's about time he received more recognition for his performance levels.

Nicolo Barella has been at the heart of Inter's recent successes on domestic soil and, for a brief moment in the 2024/25 campaign, looked as though he might help drag the Nerazurri to a Champions League trophy. While the Italian side were subsequently thrashed by Paris Saint-Germain in the final of the competition, that shouldn't understate just how good their number 23 can be.

Barella is a physical presence in the middle of the pitch for Inter, but is also a gifted creator. Typically used as a box-to-box midfielder for both club and country, new manager Christian Chivu asked him to operate as a playmaker in the 2025/26 campaign, with Barella pulling strings from deep. He's played the part to perfection so far, and continues to shine well into the new campaign.

The man who helped to orchestrate a World Cup win for Argentina in 2022, thus helping to secure Lionel Messi's status as the greatest footballer of all time. Alexis Mac Allister enjoyed a standout 2022/23 campaign for both club and country, and it was no surprise that Liverpool paid Brighton & Hove Albion the handsome fee of £35 million to sign him all those summers ago.

The player joined Liverpool in 2023 but has fond memories working alongside somebody else before that.

Mac Allister won the League Cup in his first season as a Liverpool player and hoisted the Premier League title under Arne Slot a campaign later. He suffered a slight drop in performance last season while playing for a Liverpool side that had been exposed by various teams, but there's no denying the Argentine remains an effective conductor compared to his peers, as demonstrated during the 2026 World Cup. This season, he has brought the kind of structure the Reds have lacked in the middle area, and it looks like he could be set to sign a new contract as a reward for his return to form.

Moises Caicedo was on the receiving end of plenty of criticism during his debut season in Chelsea colours. As the most expensive signing in the league's history, up until the summer of 2025, there were huge expectations placed on his young shoulders to tighten up a leaky Blues midfield instantly. He tried his best, of course, but the one-man mission often fell short.

Despite a tricky start to life at Stamford Bridge, the Ecuador destroyer picked up his performances immensely and continued to look outstanding at times last term. During a 1-0 win over Tottenham in November 2025, for example, Liverpool legend Jamie Carragher described Caicedo as "an absolute monster in midfield". Caicedo had been a regular fixture of the new regime at the club and has gone from strength to strength in west London. The only thing holding him back is his disciplinary and fitness records.

Much was made of the £107 million fee Chelsea coughed up for Enzo Fernandez as part of their midfield refurbishment – and it's perhaps not unfair to say the Argentine never fully repaid the Blues on the pitch. That said, they've now managed to make a profit on the player, selling him to Man City for £125m.

The fact that he is still so young plays into his hands. The former Benfica ace, who was born and raised in San Martin, played 170 times for the West Londoners after joining for a then-record fee in January 2023, and has now taken his Premier League experience to the Etihad. Having played in two World Cup finals, winning one, he should bring a winners' mentality to Manchester as he reunites with former Blues boss Enzo Maresca, who continues to keep the faith in him as the tough times trudge along in the winter period.

#1213. Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

What a finish from Rayan to give Bournemouth the lead! 🔥 https://t.co/9BV0G5Tqgi

The outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

The third was the same, with Evanilson chasing down a ball forward by Tyler Adams. The striker should not have got there. But Harry Maguire, captain in Fernandes’s absence, gave up, pointing at Lammens to win it. Instead, the goalkeeper was beaten to the ball and Evanilson’s finish from an angle, arcing high into the net, was superb.

"What a finish!" 😮‍💨 Evanilson makes it 3-0 to Bournemouth with a stunning goal https://t.co/hPMR78Z3cX

“You’re going down with the City,” goaded the Bournemouth fans and it is that end of the table United need to fret about. Which means, for Carrick, it has to be over. The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a new stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

“It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”

United players have said this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Telegraph columnist Jamie Carragher thinks Carrick has had enough after that.

His emotional exit after the match suggested as much, with the former Liverpool player telling Sky: “He wants to be put out of his misery tonight.”

The fact that a mid-table team can come to Old Trafford and leave with three points is no longer a surprise.

If anything, it’s unusual when competent teams struggle against United these days.

Quite how replacing a manager changes a decade of falling short solves things, who knows?

At least the scoreline is not a surprise. Bournemouth always tend to win 3-0 at Old Trafford these days

Arne Slot underwhelmed last season, and Liverpool moved swiftly to appoint Andoni Iraola from Bournemouth.

They have defeated an impressive Brighton side 2-0 today, and you can read our report here.

Former Manchester United winger Ashley Young is scathing about the players who have succeeded him.

He told Sky Sports: “Unfortunately for Michael Carrick, it’s so disappointing. The fans are behind him and backing him and of course they are, because he’s a legend of the football club.

“But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn’t run, they didn’t look like a team together.

“If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you’d swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing.”

Extraordinary scenes at the end here. Carrick walks around the pitch waving at the fans and being applauded back. It felt very much like a manager saying goodbye. As he reached the Stretford End they start singing his song and Carrick responds by banging his chest in front of them. But as soon as the manager disappeared down the tunnel the fans instantly turned on the players trailing behind. A crescendo of sustained boos reverberate around as they target the players and make their feelings quite clear.

Picking Fernandes on the bench meant that Carrick got to snub him, but it also means that Sky get to make a point of his efforts to express himself, which does not really help the situation.

The away side now match Manchester City and Liverpool.

Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Antonio Conte, Julian Nagelsmann and Kieran McKenna are all in the frame to succeed Carrick if things go south soon.

What is striking is that none of the options are convincingly capable of such a vast, difficult task. That’s not their fault - it’s the owners’.

That’s the opinion of at least one managerial candidate linked with the United gig, should Carrick be given a healthy sum to walk away and take up an interest in koi carp.

With Fernandes dropped, that moment has probably got closer.

He writes: “A source close to one of United’s managerial candidates said: ‘It’s clear they need order and discipline. The dressing room is out of control and that is the first thing to fix.’

“That view was echoed by a friend of another candidate, who said: ‘The players talk too much. United is one of the biggest clubs in the world and that has to be respected.’”

Carrick had hinted as much in his pre-weekend press conference.

Fernandes’ zesty outburst, where he said United’s tactical failings against Como were “on the manager and staff” has understandably seen his position as United captain questioned.

Carrick did not rule it out, saying: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

#1211. 'Incredible' Moment Bruno Fernandes 'Assisted' His Own Man Utd Goal

It was a frustrating night for Manchester United in the Champions League, as the English side were held to a 2-2 draw against Sporting CP.

After losing his first outing against Liverpool, Mauricio Pochettino was unable to get a win in his next game despite having the lead late on. Luis Suarez opened the scoring in the first half, bagging a penalty after missing another one just three minutes prior.

The Red Devils won their own penalty after the break, with Lisandro Martinez fouled and Bruno Fernandes stepping up from 12 yards. The club captain then put Man Utd ahead, scoring a strange goal just two minutes later.

With 10 minutes to play, Senne Lammens then made a huge blunder, dropping a simple catch, allowing Suarez to acrobatically score an equaliser. The game ended 2-2, with both teams walking away with a point.

While there is much to talk about in terms of Man Utd's overall performance, there was one specific moment in the game which has separately generated a lot of interest.

Having scored his penalty, Fernandes then took a speculative shot on goal only moments later. His left-footed strike from all of 25 yards didn't look likely to trouble Kaique Pereira, but it somehow beat the Sporting goalkeeper.

Replays showed that the ball had hit a divot in the Estadio Jose Alvalade turf, causing Fernandes' shot to pop up and fly into the back of the net. On the commentary for TNT Sports, Ally McCoist summed things up, stating:

"That's extraordinary, it really is. That's incredible."

The Man Utd goalkeeper was poor, but another played has drawn the anger of his own support.

After the match, the TNT Sports pundits then analysed the goal with new footage showing exactly how the goal came about. Incredible footage captured what happened to the turf, showing that Fernandes had managed to make a divot in the ground just seconds before taking on the strike.

The Man Utd captain surely didn't do it on purpose, but because of his prior ground scuffing, he essentially managed to assist his second goal. Indeed, were it not for the disruption to the turf, his effort surely would never have beatenthe Sporting goalkeeper.

Pundit and former Man Utd star Owen Hargreaves joked:

"This is the assist of the season. The best assist I’ve never seen."

Hargreaves went on to add: "What a bounce that is; the goalkeeper's got absolutely no chance. The one thing I would say is, watch this bounce... unbelievable, it's like a golf divot."

Fernandes certainly had a huge slice of good fortune with his goal, but Man Utd weren't able to make the most of it, conceding a preventable equaliser. They face RB Leipzig next time out in the Champions League.

Former Liverpool defender Carragher has been blown away by Isak so far this season, praising the forward's improvement outside of scoring goals.
