#1155. NWSL announces new player development rule to incentivize youth investment, aims for further expansion

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest week on the NWSL calendar is here as the buildup towards the 2026 NWSL Championship is underway. An awards show, countless events, and media days were all on the agenda ahead of Saturday's big game. That included the annual state of the league by commissioner Jessica Berman on Thursday.

This year, the commissioner welcomed media to the NWSL Championship in Washington, D.C., and celebrated record ticket sales, attendance, and future expansion ahead of Saturday night's championship between the Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current, live on CBS at 8 p.m. ET. She also announced a few new league rules and future match events.

The commissioner introduced the new player development rule. While the league previously submitted paperwork for a potential future second=division league, conversation and planning around that is currently paused with the upcoming 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and efforts to grow NWSL in other ways.

"As we grow from 16 to 18 teams in 2028, we know that we have to prioritize the pipeline, not just the pipeline of players, but the pipeline of talent that supports the players in the daily training environment. One of the things that makes the United States so uniquely positioned in the global women's soccer landscape is the depth of that potential pipeline," said Berman in her opening remarks.

"That's why today we're announcing the NWSL Player Development Rule. It's an important step in strengthening the pathway to professional soccer for the next generation of players. The rule creates actual incentives for clubs to invest in identifying, developing, and retaining young talent, and it gives the clubs the flexibility to design their programs in the way that makes sense with their sporting philosophies."

More information and the types of incentives will roll out for clubs as the new player development rule goes into effect, but it is another step in future roster-building for clubs now alongside general player signings, transfers, the High Impact Player rule, and the Under-18 mechanism.

The addition of the rule is paving the way for more support staff and systems in place. The commissioner also announced the new NWSL Sporting Executive Program, meant to provide more support for club leadership development. The inaugural set of leadership includes six executives from the league who will participate in the program.

"Developing the future of the sport is not just limited to the players; it's also about the technical staff who surround those players each and every day ... this is a first-of-its-kind program invested in talent, and it was curated and developed in collaboration with U.S. Soccer and FIFA. This new year-long initiative will provide sporting executives at our clubs with curated, specialized education, mentorship, and leadership development opportunities tailored around the unique demands of our league and the women's professional game," she said.

The NWSL commissioner then announced the future site of the next NWSL Challenge Cup. The 2027 NWSL Challenge Cup will take place in Austin, Texas, next summer.

The tournament has evolved since its first iteration as a placeholder for the COVID-19-affected season and is now a unique one-off marquee match between top clubs, typically the NWSL Shield titleholders and the NWSL Championship winners. In years where one club wins both, the game is a rematch of the previous NWSL Championship match.

"Following the success of this year's Challenge Cup in Columbus, where we took the event to a neutral site to give an opportunity to introduce the NWSL to a new community," she said.

The 2026 NWSL Challenge Cup was between 2025 NWSL Shield winners Kansas City Current and 2025 NWSL Championship winners Gotham FC. The 2026 competition was held in Columbus, Ohio. The state will now welcome its first NWSL franchise in 2028 alongside another expansion club in Atlanta.

Fans will undoubtedly make the connection and wonder if there is a future where an NWSL club calls Austin home. Currently, there are three NWSL clubs in California and only one in Texas, the Houston Dash.

"We're really excited to create another special experience for our fans and our players while making the NWSL a place that can invite new audiences," Berman said about heading to Austin.

Commissioner Berman celebrated the league's recent return to the nation's capital for another NWSL Championship. The city hosted the 2022 event and now returns four years later with more attention on the league, the clubs, and its players than ever before.

"Today, we're bigger, stronger, more visible, and more ambitious than ever before, and the next five years are going to redefine what's possible. We have an extraordinary opportunity in front of us, and we intend to seize it," she said.

Two incoming clubs set for 2028 and new player roster rules are just the beginning of NWSL's next chapter. There's still the potential for more clubs on the horizon, and current clubs Houston Dash and Racing Louisville are in the process of vetting for a sale to new ownership as franchise entry fees into the league are booming to new heights.

And of course, there is still the biggest game of the year to play on Saturday.

"The Washington Spirit are back in the championship for the third consecutive year, determined to bring home that title. And standing in their way is the Kansas City Current, with its own ambitions to win a championship after winning the Shield in 2025. These are two exceptional clubs, two incredibly passionate fan base, and the championship is still to be decided, [we're] very excited about the rest of this week."

#1154. MLS Cup bracket predictions: Lionel Messi's Inter Miami set for repeat?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's time for some brackets as the MLS Cup playoffs are upon us. With the Wild Card round kicking off on Thursday night, 18 teams (still too many) will enter the gauntlet that is the playoffs. All eyes will be on Nashville SC, who have a first-round bye after winning the Supporters' Shield and setting a new MLS regular-season points record with 77 points. However, when it comes down to it, anyone can fall in a one-off match, as being successful in the regular season is a different proposition than doing so in the postseason.

While the Wild Card round is a one-off, win-or-go-home match, the first round is a best-of-three series with games going to a penalty shootout if tied. That can change the calculus a bit, especially for teams getting an early goal in the first game, since there are still two more chances to advance. But since there are playoffs, that also means that we have to predict the bracket, so let's get to it.

The Seattle Sounders come into this postseason in a tough spot. While they've become a team that can't be counted out of MLS Cup contention, they enter the playoffs without one of their best defenders. Center back Jackson Ragen was suspended for two games following a disciplinary review for his challenge on Los Angeles FC's Jacob Shaffelburg. While the Sounders have returned to health, this opens the door for Real Salt Lake to get out of the Wild Card round.

In Orlando, this is one of the matchups of the entire playoffs as Evander and Antoine Griezmann will battle in a match where defense is optional. Both teams had higher ambitions heading into the season, so for the loser, it could have major implications. But after winning Newcomer of the Year, Griezmann, alongside Orlando's strong attack, will prove to be too much to handle for Cincinnati as we head to the first round of the playoffs proper.

The parity in MLS this season, especially in the Western Conference, is real. You could tell me that anyone would come out of the West, and it's believable. Vancouver may be the team to beat, but needing to replace Sebastian Berhalter and Andres Cubas midseason did hurt the squad. Jesper Sorensen has done plenty to keep Vancouver afloat, but they're still vulnerable, although that'll be more of an issue in later rounds depending on how the bracket shakes out. St. Louis City SC have already exceeded expectations by winning the U.S. Open Cup, and if Alexandru Matan is on his game, they may be unbeatable, but they can run hot and cold. Add in Bruce Arena still evolving with the league and the cardiac kids of Dallas (and of course the brilliance of Petar Musa), and that brings us to the advancing sides. I would apologize to Los Angeles FC, but post-Steve Cherundolo, this is a side that has faltered, and a long look needs to be taken at the squad following the season to move forward.

In the East, we're in B.J. Callaghan's world. Los Angeles FC are the last team to do the double of winning the Supporters' Shield and MLS Cup, and it's a tough thing for Nashville to do, but this team has only allowed 25 goals in a full season. They can score, they can grind a game to a halt, and they have so many ways to give the opposition fits. In a best-of-three, good luck getting past them. Speaking of slowing a game down, the New England Revolution are a worst-case matchup for the fighting Cavan Sullivans of Philadelphia. Joshua Wynder has stabilized the defense in front of Matt Turner, and while the Revolution may not have a high ceiling as constructed, the floor is so high in this unique setup. Charlotte facing Chicago might as well be a coin flip. Then there's Miami facing Columbus. Like the Union, the Crew can win because their attacking upside is so high, and Miami are a flawed team, but Lionel Messi is still doing Lionel Messi things. As long as that's the case, I'm rarely going to bet against the Herons.

Now the playoffs really are getting underway. These are one-off games where the best of the best are going up against each other. San Jose's run comes to an end here, while St. Louis and Dallas fight in an evenly matched clash to determine who else comes out of the Western Conference. Nashville's defense again puts up a suffocating performance to get past Charlotte, and Messi drives Inter Miami past the Revolution, setting up a fascinating set of conference finals.

Okay, I swear that this wasn't supposed to go chalk with three of the top four finishers in the regular season making it to the conference finals, but getting to the end of the season and saying that the good teams are actually good shouldn't be revolutionary. Thomas Muller and Brian White are enough to push the Whitecaps to the MLS Cup final, where the Eastern Conference yet again comes down to Messi versus Hany Mukhtar. Nashville may be the better-coached team, but Miami have found a way with their backs against the wall to produce a rematch of last season's MLS Cup final.

Participants: Vancouver Whitecaps, Inter MiamiWinners: Inter Miami

Hey, it's Messi and Muller, just like we're having a top-tier Champions League matchup. It has been a playoff gauntlet, but the more things change, the more they stay the same. Muller and Messi have faced each other 11 times, with Muller claiming seven wins to Messi's four. However, after getting one over on Muller last season, Messi isn't going to let a chance at a second consecutive MLS Cup pass by, even if this one is in Vancouver amid the uncertain future of BC Place as the home of the Whitecaps.

#1153. Spurs win three in row for first time in 616 days to pile pressure on Sage

For the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

Spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

“I am really aware of the situation,” Sage said. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”

The decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

It was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

It was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

Jean-Philippe Mateta receives his first red card for Crystal Palace! 🟥 https://t.co/U9UYb29mbk

All of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

“Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi said. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We showed our maturity. We are improving.”

The second goal was always coming and it arrived in the 73rd minute, when Van Hecke attacked a wonderful cross by Mateus Fernandes. Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson saved the first attempt but the ball dropped onto the head of Van Hecke, now seated in the six-yard box, and he happily nodded it home.

Jan Paul van Hecke doubles Spurs' lead! 👊 https://t.co/1Odkkr8wBJ

The new signings at Spurs endured a difficult first few weeks but there were more signs here that they are adjusting to De Zerbi’s system. Sandro Tonali was exceptional in midfield and teenage talent Luca Williams-Barnett also sparkled off the bench. “Tonali was unbelievable,” De Zerbi said. “We played with two players more: Tonali was double.”

Spurs face Leeds United, Ipswich Town, Sunderland and Fulham in their next four league games. The momentum could, and perhaps should, continue to build. Their optimism here contrasted sharply with the angst of Palace, and with the troubled look that was etched on Sage’s face.

“Very pleased for the performance, very tough game. You don’t know 11 [against 11] would be different game but Crystal Palace are very tough because they defend with a low block, no space and we showed we are a mature team. Maybe we could score more goals with more nastiness, but I am very happy because we created many chances. We need more goals for sure. It’s not enough, but we are improving a lot.

“I was very nervous before the game, during the game, after the red card, it’s always better playing with one player more. But today, against this team, they played with this behaviour, all behind the line of the ball, aggressive. Very tough game.”

When asked if Spurs are looking up the table, he replied: “We don’t forget the ambitions. We have to look behind what was the situation two weeks ago. In the last two years, two times 17th in the table, many games without a win in front of our fans. We have to stay focused. They are improving, increasing the level of performance.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Palace defender said: “Definitely was frustrating. It was one of the first tackles of the game. And we felt like we were doing well and it is unfortunate. We go again.

“The main message was don’t concede again, stay tight as a defence and try to hit them on the counter. That is the best plan when you’re down a man.

“Unfortunately, it didn’t happen today. We know what we can do as a team, as a back five, the whole unit. There were some positives in the games, but I can’t say much when you lose. We just have to go again.

“Hopefully, the next game we win. The main message is to stay together as a team. We know what we are capable of. It is staying confident and bouncing back.”

While Tottenham are chasing a third successive league victory for the first time in 616 day, De Zerbi insisted there will be no complacency. “For me nothing has changed. We started this pre-season with a long project and we have to stay calm and clear in the head to work to build something better than when we came here,” he said. “One win or one defeat more, nothing will change. We have to analyse to improve the results but to improve the results we have to improve all aspects.”

Pierre Sage, the Palace manager, lightened the load after knocking Fulham out of the Carabao Cup in midweek but seemed surprised that the fans have remained so supportive. “It’s always a good sign,” he said. “I appreciate it [singing his name at Craven Cottage] very much and I can thank them but I prefer they are with the team than me alone. Because I’m the manager, but I’m not the most important part of the team, of the performance and the result. I think the players need it more than me but it’s really appreciated from me.”

Asked what he has learnt about fan sentiment from looking at social media, he said: “I think they understood what happened, why we are not perfect at the moment. We don’t care who is the most responsible for the situation. I take the responsibility. I have no problem with that. I just want people to understand what we do and why.”

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Tottenham and Crystal Palace.

Last weekend, Spurs enjoyed a historic result, beating Chelsea 2-0 at Stamford Bridge for only the second time in the league for 36 years thanks to Mike Penders’ own goal and Mathys Tel’s stunning solo strike. This result, coupled with the 3-1 victory over Coventry City in their previous home outing, means that Tottenham have won back-to-back league games and are beginning to gather some momentum under Roberto De Zerbi.

In his pre-match press conference, when asked if he’s felt a change in atmosphere after the triumph at Stamford Bridge, De Zerbi replied: “We have not achieved our goal. We want our fans to be happy, not now, at the end of the season. Now we have to push, we have to stay focused, we have to increase the spirit, the appetite to win games in a row. To do that, we have to show if we are good enough. If we are good enough on the pitch, for sure we are ready. In the head, in the mentality, we have to show, because the step of this club is to win games in a row and to be angry day by day, game by game, win by win. One time or two times are not enough.”

Palace have endured a tricky and inconsistent start to the season under their summer appointment Pierre Sage, accumulating just seven points from their opening seven league matches while shipping 17 goals. The 1-0 League Cup victory over Fulham in midweek has momentarily eased the pressure on the Frenchman, but given their newfound success in recent campaigns, fan expectations have risen, with recent performances prompting some cause for concern.

Tottenham remain without the suspended Rodrigo Bentancur, while Xavi Simons, Wilson Odobert, Lucas Bergvall, Savio, Tosin Adarabioyo and Mykhaylo Mudryk are out injured. James Maddison was substituted early in the second half at Chelsea with an apparent groin strain, but De Zerbi insists he’s available for this one. Destiny Udogie could also be involved after recovering from a knee issue.

The visitors are without the injured trio of Ismaila Sarr, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chadi Riad, but there’s hope that Quinten Timber and Jorgen Strand Larsen are fit to be involved this evening after they both missed the Fulham victory.

Kick-off is at 17:30, with teams coming shortly.

#1152. Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Heterochromatin typically represses genes1,2, yet some genes paradoxically require it for activation3,4,5,6,7. How can the same chromatin environment both silence and promote transcription? Here we address this question by interrogating the clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus, where subsets of genes are stochastically expressed while most remain silent8. In neurons, stochastic and combinatorial expression of Pcdh genes generates unique cell-surface barcodes required for self–non-self discrimination and neural circuit assembly8. By combining RNA labelling of Pcdh genes and neurodevelopmental cell types with single-molecule chromatin tracing and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, we find that a compact heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh genes forms as these genes become activated during development. Pcdh transcription occurs within the compact domain and reads through downstream genes, and distal enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters. Genetic perturbations in mice suggest that opposing genome folding forces cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote stochastic Pcdh expression. Specifically, while DNA loop extrusion allows enhancers to breach heterochromatin and find target promoters, heterochromatin-driven compartmentalization supports an expanded enhancer–promoter search space. These findings shed light on a process foundational to the development of vertebrate nervous systems and suggest a mechanism for how transcription can occur within seemingly silent chromatin environments.

Histone H3 lysine 9 (H3 K9) trimethylation, a canonical post-translational modification of constitutive heterochromatin, is known to spread over large genomic territories and repress gene expression9. These defining properties of heterochromatin were recognized in classic position–effect variegation studies in Drosophila during the 1930s, in which euchromatic genes placed near domains with trimethylated H3 K9 (H3K9me3) became transcriptionally silenced1,2. However, subsequent discovery of genes whose expression depends on their residence within heterochromatin revealed that this conflict is not absolute. For example, expression of the light (lt) and rolled (rl) genes in flies requires their position within pericentromeric heterochromatin3,4,5. In mice and humans, proper expression of olfactory receptor (OR) and KRAB domain-containing zinc-finger protein (KZFP) genes also depends on H3K9me3 heterochromatin6,7. These ‘escapee’ genes suggest the existence of specialized regulatory strategies that allow transcription to occur within, or despite, heterochromatin, raising fundamental questions about when heterochromatin facilitates versus restrains gene expression.

The vertebrate clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus provides a striking example of a large gene family whose expression has been proposed to require escape from a heterochromatic environment10,11,12,13. Pcdh genes are expressed predominantly in neurons, where they govern neuronal self–non-self discrimination and circuit formation8. In individual neurons, only a small subset of Pcdh genes are expressed, whereas most remain silent8. Because selection of Pcdh genes is random and combinatorial14,15,16,17, this process generates extraordinary cell surface protein isoform diversity that marks each neuron with a unique identity, or ‘barcode’. Neurites presenting the same Pcdh barcode recognize and avoid one another, thereby preventing self-adhesion, whereas neurites presenting distinct Pcdh barcodes do not self-recognize and can interact18,19,20. Consistent with their critical role in neural circuit assembly, genetic variants in Pcdh genes are associated with neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, including autism spectrum disorder21,22 and schizophrenia23.

In mice, there are 58 Pcdh genes distributed across three tandemly arranged clusters—α (Pcdha), β (Pcdhb) and γ (Pcdhg)—spanning roughly 1 megabase of DNA on chromosome 18 (ref. 24) (Fig. 1a). Pcdha genes are regulated by the HS5-1 enhancer located downstream of the Pcdha cluster, whereas Pcdhb and Pcdhg genes are regulated by the HS18-22 and HS16-17 enhancers, respectively, located downstream of the Pcdhg cluster25 (Fig. 1a). The Pcdha and Pcdhg genes are further subdivided into ‘alternate’ and ‘c-type’ isoforms24 (Fig. 1a). Pcdh genes and their promoters are marked by H3 K9 trimethylation and CpG DNA methylation (5mC)10,13,26. Stochastic Pcdh gene choice requires promoter DNA demethylation driven by cohesin-mediated enhancer–promoter interactions, with promoter demethylation leading to CTCF binding and sustained transcription of the respective Pcdh gene10,13,15,27,28. Although these findings have identified how Pcdh promoters escape DNA methylation, they do not address how euchromatic Pcdh enhancers navigate H3K9me3 heterochromatin to activate silent Pcdh promoters. Several questions remain unanswered. Specifically, do stochastic enhancer–promoter interactions occur within heterochromatin? Is Pcdh transcription carried out within a heterochromatic environment otherwise programmed to suppress gene activity, or must Pcdh loci escape this environment to transcribe? And, does heterochromatin contribute to the stochasticity of Pcdh promoter choice?

To answer these questions, we sought a single-molecule view of Pcdh locus architecture during development that included the positioning of active and inactive promoters. Until now, most insights into this relationship have come from bulk genomic analyses. At a locus where only a few genes are active while most remain silent, bulk measurements mainly reflect the non-chosen genes, effectively averaging out the features of the chosen ones. To circumvent this limitation, we used optical reconstruction of chromatin architecture (ORCA), a single-molecule chromatin tracing assay29, in olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) of the mouse olfactory epithelium (OE). We selected OSNs for three reasons. First, they undergo multiple stages of development and constantly regenerate, such that each stage is present within the OE simultaneously. Second, Pcdh gene expression is developmentally regulated during OSN maturation15,20, with approximately one gene per cluster expressed from each allele in mature OSNs (mOSNs) (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Third, stochastic expression of Pcdh genes has a critical role in OSN axon wiring and odour map formation20,30,31.

We designed ORCA probes that tile the Pcdh locus in 90 10-kilobase bins, omitting repetitive and GC-poor regions (Fig. 1a). ORCA probes were validated in OE sections from mice in which mOSNs were genetically labelled (Extended Data Fig. 2a). We visualized ORCA data as contact frequency matrices, which depict the frequency that each pair of locus positions (bins along the Pcdh locus) falls within a specified three-dimensional (3D) distance across all imaged traces. We set this threshold near the average distance between adjacent locus positions in an experiment. The contact frequency map obtained from ORCA correlated strongly with chromosome conformation capture Hi-C data of the same genomic bins from sorted mOSNs (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c, Pearson’s r = 0.87), and the correlation remained high across a sweep of ORCA contact thresholds (Extended Data Fig. 2d). ORCA data from whole OE tissue also remained consistent across separate experiments (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f, Pearson’s r = 0.98) and showed good detection efficiency across locus positions (Extended Data Fig. 2g). These results demonstrate that ORCA faithfully captures Pcdh locus architecture.

To study how Pcdh locus architecture changes during Pcdh gene activation and neuronal maturation, we combined ORCA imaging of Pcdh DNA with RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) labelling of the five major OSN developmental cell stages: horizontal basal cells (HBCs), globose basal cells (GBCs), immediate neuronal precursors (INPs), immature OSNs (iOSNs) and mOSNs (Fig. 1c). This lineage spawns from the mitotic HBC population located near the basal surface of the OE. As OSNs progress along their developmental axis, these cells migrate towards the apical surface of the OE (Fig. 1c). RNA labelling of marker genes for each stage reflected this basal-to-apical migration (Fig. 1d). We also stained samples with fluorescently tagged wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), a lectin that binds cell membranes, to obtain 3D segmentations of cells in the OE (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We mapped both RNA and Pcdh DNA puncta to these segmentations, then classified ORCA traces (that is, individual DNA paths) into different developmental stages on the basis of the RNA signal of the cells in which they resided (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c).

The contact frequency maps for each stage of OSN development illustrated two trends. First, stripes denoting contacts between Pcdh enhancers and their target promoters became more prominent as cells matured (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1d–f). Second, contacts between locus positions containing Pcdhb genes and the alternate genes from the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, as well as the 60-kilobase stretch upstream of the Pcdha genes, increased (Fig. 1e,f). Subtracting the contact frequency map of each developmental stage from the mOSN map emphasized that these inter-cluster contacts constituted the most pronounced changes in locus architecture over development (Fig. 1e).

The formation of these inter-cluster contact domains was reminiscent of the checkerboard pattern created by compartmentalization of active and repressed chromatin domains seen on Hi-C maps32. Given that this compartmentalization is mainly driven by homotypic interactions between heterochromatic regions of the genome, we hypothesized that the locus regions engaging in these contacts would have histone marks characteristic of heterochromatin. To investigate this possibility, we performed quantitative native chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (nChIP–seq) for H3K9me3 in FACS-isolated HBCs and mOSNs. In HBCs, the Pcdh locus was lightly coated in H3K9me3, with H3K9me3 levels increasing roughly threefold in mOSNs (Fig. 1g,h). Furthermore, in mOSNs, two major stretches of enriched H3K9me3 emerged separated by regions devoid of H3K9me3 between and beyond them (Fig. 1g). Specifically, the DNA regions of the Pcdh locus that engaged in inter-cluster contacts over OSN development became heavily coated with H3K9me3, whereas regions of the locus containing Pcdh c-type genes and enhancers remained free of H3K9me3 (Fig. 1e,g). We hereafter refer to the H3K9me3-marked chromatin regions engaging in inter-cluster contacts as the ‘heterochromatin domain’ of the Pcdh locus. This definition indicates the spatial arrangement of the regions within the Pcdh locus that are marked by H3K9me3 in OSNs. We refer to the regions of the locus not marked by H3K9me3 containing Pcdh c-type genes and enhancers as euchromatin.

To understand the positioning of the heterochromatin domain within the architecture of the Pcdh locus, we calculated the distance of each locus position to the geometric centre of its respective trace and examined the median over all traces across each stage of development. All locus positions moved closer to the geometric centre as cells matured, indicating a general compaction of the locus (Fig. 1i). Layered on top of this trend, locus positions belonging to the heterochromatin domain moved closest to the centre (Fig. 1i, boxed regions), whereas euchromatic regions remained further in the periphery. To better quantify the degree of compaction of the heterochromatin domain, we measured its radius of gyration (Rg), a metric commonly used to describe the volume of a polymer, and found that Rg decreases as neurons mature (Fig. 1j). Surprisingly, as compaction increases, so does the number of genes expressed per cell from within the domain (Fig. 1j). We further visualized these changes in locus architecture by plotting individual traces coloured by regions that become heterochromatic or euchromatic over development and by examining single-molecule distance maps (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4). Despite heterogeneity across traces, the formation of the domain was evident: in HBCs, both regions tended to occupy large and intermixed volumes, whereas in mOSNs, the regions segregated, with heterochromatin forming a dense, more centrally located domain and euchromatin occupying more open volumes in the periphery (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4).

Overall, these results indicate that in neural stem cells, the Pcdh locus is lightly coated with H3K9me3 heterochromatin, yet open and intermixed, with a compact heterochromatin domain forming in its centre as cells mature into post-mitotic neurons (Fig. 1l). Counterintuitively, the formation of this compact structure coincides with activation of Pcdh genes (Fig. 1j).

These results could be explained by the presence of two distinct subpopulations—actively transcribing loci that transiently lose heterochromatin and silent loci that do not. Alternatively, actively transcribing loci could retain heterochromatin and their compacted architecture. Because our bulk measurements of H3K9me3 by nChIP–seq could not distinguish between these two possibilities, we turned to stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM) to measure H3K9me3 in single cells. We combined STORM for H3K9me3 with RNA FISH labelling of Pcdh isoforms and OSN cell types, as well as ORCA imaging of DNA, to test for colocalization of heterochromatin with transcribing Pcdh alleles (Fig. 2a). We used RNA probes against 11 Pcdh isoforms and confirmed their specificity for their target isoforms in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b).

Overlaying Pcdh RNA staining on Pcdh DNA loci labelled by ORCA revealed DNA traces that colocalized with RNA puncta (Extended Data Fig. 6a). By measuring distances between Pcdh loci and Pcdh RNA puncta, we identified a data-driven distance threshold below which RNA transcripts could be classified as nascent (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c). RNA puncta within this threshold were brighter than those beyond it, consistent with nascent transcriptional bursting33 (Extended Data Fig. 6d).

We then examined the spatial relationship between transcribing Pcdh DNA loci and H3K9me3 STORM signal in mOSNs. Remarkably, we observed many examples of nascent transcription occurring at Pcdh loci that colocalized with H3K9me3 STORM (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Plotting the ORCA traces of these loci alongside H3K9me3 STORM localizations revealed transcribing promoters spatially residing within heterochromatin (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 7a).

To assess whether STORM captured a nuclear enrichment of H3K9me3 over the Pcdh locus, we quantified the number of H3K9me3 localizations surrounding Pcdh loci relative to randomized positions within the same nuclei. The median number of H3K9me3 localizations detected around Pcdh DNA loci exceeded that of randomized positions in 999 of 1,000 simulations (empirical P = 0.002) (Fig. 2c). We performed the same analyses on Tex15 loci, which are not marked by H3K9me3 as assayed by bulk nChIP–seq (Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). We used Tex15 nascent RNA transcripts as proxies for Tex15 DNA positions (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). In contrast to Pcdh loci, Tex15 loci did not show an enrichment for H3K9me3 (empirical P = 0.292) (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Furthermore, we observed more Tex15 loci lacking any H3K9me3 signal compared with Pcdh loci (Extended Data Fig. 7e).

We next asked whether Pcdh transcription was associated with reduced local H3K9me3 signal and domain compaction by first dividing loci into those with or without detectable nascent transcription, the latter of which we hereafter refer to as non-transcribing. We then measured the number of H3K9me3 STORM localizations around these loci and the Rg of their heterochromatin domains by ORCA. Surprisingly, transcribing Pcdh loci had slightly higher H3K9me3 STORM signal and slightly more compact heterochromatin domains relative to non-transcribing loci (Fig. 2d,e). Furthermore, transcription of individual Pcdh genes was associated neither with a change in H3K9me3 STORM signal around transcribing promoters, at the resolution of our assay, nor with a change in heterochromatin domain compaction (Fig. 2f,g).

Overall, these analyses indicate that transcription of Pcdh loci can occur in H3K9me3-rich nuclear territories and does not disrupt the heterochromatin domain of the locus.

These data prompted us to further evaluate features of a transcribing Pcdh locus. To do that, we expanded the design of our RNA probes to a total of 31 Pcdh genes that showed appreciable staining and specificity (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). We noted that nascently transcribing RNA puncta often colocalized with other Pcdh RNAs of the same cluster (Fig. 3a), and more nascent puncta were detected for progressively downstream isoforms at the Pcdha and Pcdhg, but not Pcdhb, clusters (Fig. 3b). Meanwhile, mature transcript levels measured by bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) remained relatively flat across all clusters (Fig. 3b). We reasoned that these results could reflect nascent transcription of Pcdha and Pcdhg genes that reads through downstream isoforms (Fig. 3c). Yet, the number of nascent Pcdh RNAs detected at a locus was not associated with changes in heterochromatin domain Rg (Fig. 3d), indicating that this putative transcriptional readthrough occurs without domain decompaction.

To identify features of locus architecture associated with transcription, we subtracted the contact frequency maps of non-transcribing loci from the maps of transcribing loci in mOSNs. This revealed an enrichment of enhancer–promoter contacts in transcribing loci (Fig. 3e–g), which was further supported by an increase in transcription probability as a function of enhancer–promoter proximity (Extended Data Fig. 8). For Pcdha and Pcdhg genes, these enhancer–promoter contact enrichments included promoters upstream of the transcribing isoform, and the magnitude of enrichment experienced by each promoter diminished when filtering on transcription of progressively downstream isoforms (Fig. 3e,g). By contrast, Pcdhb promoters had more local enhancer-contact enrichments upon transcription (Fig. 3f).

Together, these data indicate that at the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, transcription of chosen promoters reads through downstream genes. This pattern is consistent with splicing of Pcdha and Pcdhg variable exons to three small constant exons located 3′ of these clusters34, and was not observed at the Pcdhb cluster, which lacks constant exons. Furthermore, these data indicate that Pcdh gene choice is driven by highly specific enhancer–promoter interactions across this multi-gene, multi-enhancer locus.

We next asked where Pcdh transcription and enhancer–promoter interactions occur within the spatial architecture of the locus (Fig. 1l) and, in particular, whether transcribing promoters remain within or exit the heterochromatin domain. To assess the positioning of transcribing promoters, we measured the distances between promoters and heterochromatic locus positions in the presence and absence of transcription in mOSNs (Fig. 4a). These distances did not change during transcription (Fig. 4a). On the other hand, distances between promoters and euchromatic locus positions decreased during transcription (Fig. 4a). This effect seemed driven by decreased distances between promoters and enhancers upon transcription (Fig. 4b). These results indicate that enhancer–promoter contacts associated with transcription bring euchromatic locus positions closer to the heterochromatin domain, but neither these contacts nor transcription itself cause transcribing promoters to exit the domain. Plotting transcription probability as a function of a promoter’s distance to the heterochromatin centre supported this conclusion, as promoters were most likely to be transcribing at distances within the median Rg of the heterochromatin domain (Fig. 4c).
